Upper Sioux Community

Upper Sioux Community, also presented as Pezihutazizi Oyate, is a distinct Dakota government in the Minnesota River region. A 2025 state guide carries the Community's narrative, including its establishment, government and land return. An older first-person account provides context. Reading their dates together helps preserve continuity without treating changing figures as contradictions to erase.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Homeland, return and government

The Community account describes homeland relationships, forced removal and return. The 2025 profile places the Community's establishment in 1938 and discusses its 1995 constitution, enterprises and services. These publications carry a community narrative through state institutions; they are not independent verification of every historical assertion. This starting selection does not establish all present laws or membership rules. The linked tribal-government website returned 403 in the original review, so its own inaccessible body is not claimed as inspected or treated as a paywall.

Read the sources [1] Minnesota Secretary of State; the profile presents the Upper Sioux Community’s account [2] Minnesota Indian Affairs Council; page uses first-person community language and links to the Upper Sioux Community

02

Land return and dated accounts

The 2025 profile describes the 2024 return of former Upper Sioux Agency State Park lands. A 2017 landscape photograph provides a view of that named place before the transfer, rather than an image of current access arrangements. The older Indian Affairs page and newer guide contain different acreage and population figures. Their dates and scopes are retained; neither supplies a current census or an exact Indigenous homeland boundary. Further work should follow the transfer records and Community interpretation while leaving sensitive places and cultural knowledge out of public description.

Government / community historical accountMinnesota Secretary of State; the profile presents the Upper Sioux Community’s accountSource 1

Minnesota Tribal Government 2025 — Upper Sioux Community / Pezihutazizi Oyate profile ↗

Publication: 2025 edition

This two-page community profile describes the Minnesota River homeland, the community’s establishment in 1938, its 1995 constitution, tribal enterprises and services, and the 2024 return of former Upper Sioux Agency State Park lands. The state publication carries the community’s narrative; it is not an independent verification of every historical statement. Its 577 membership figure and 3,725-acre land-base statement are dated to the report and are not current 2026 measurements or an Indigenous homeland boundary.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete Upper Sioux Community profile, pp. 9–10 (PDF lines 347–381), including the paragraphs on homeland, 1938 community formation, governance, economic development and services, and the 2024 transfer. The remaining tribal profiles and state agency listings were not counted as Dakota-community evidence.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Government / contextual referenceMinnesota Indian Affairs Council; page uses first-person community language and links to the Upper Sioux CommunitySource 2Supporting reference · outside substantive inspected count

Pezihutazizi / Oyate — Upper Sioux Community historical page ↗

Publication: Undated; accessed 2026

The page preserves a first-person historical account of homeland, forced removal, return, government formation, enterprises and services. Its undated population and acreage statements (453 people and over 900 acres) differ from the 2025 state guide’s account of a 2024 land return and 3,725-acre total land base. These figures should be read as dated versions of a community narrative rather than treated as current or as evidence of a boundary. The linked Upper Sioux government site returned HTTP 403 to the research request; no access control was bypassed.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Read the full historical body and its links to elected leaders and the Upper Sioux Community website (page lines 16–36). The linked community site itself was not accessible from this request; its 403 response is not classified as a reader paywall.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026
